analysis.one_liner: Toughens coal mine safety rules: rescue chambers, underground communications, lower dust limits, and bigger fines for repeat violators.
analysis.headline: The House passed the S-MINER Act 214-199 in January 2008, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten safety rules in the nation's coal mines after a series of fatal disasters. It requires rescue chambers within 500 feet of where miners work, communication and tracking systems to find trapped miners, half the current limit on explosive coal dust, and fines up to $250,000 for mine operators with repeated safety violations. It also creates a confidential complaint office for miners and orders independent investigations when multiple miners are killed.
analysis.who_benefits: Underground coal miners and their families gain the most: better odds of surviving an explosion, less black lung disease from dust, protection from being disciplined for reporting hazards, and an ombudsman to take their complaints confidentially. Communities near mines gain from a 24-hour federal emergency call center and public maps of operating and abandoned mines.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each underground coal mine to install portable rescue chambers or sealed refuge shelters within 500 feet of the nearest working face, and bars operators from satisfying the breathable-air requirement merely by placing an order for future delivery of a chamber.

Requires emergency response plans to include post-accident communication between underground and surface personnel and electronic tracking so surface crews can locate miners trapped underground, with systems hardened to survive a disaster.

Cuts the permissible respirable coal dust level in half, from 2.0 to 1.0 milligrams per cubic meter, moves compliance sampling from mine operators to federal inspectors using tamper-resistant personal dust monitors, and sets a new silica dust limit — measures aimed at black lung disease.

Authorizes fines of $50,000 to $250,000 for a pattern of safety violations, requires withdrawing all miners from such a mine until violations are fixed, and raises the maximum penalty per serious violation to $150,000, with corporate owners jointly liable.

Creates a Miner Ombudsman in the Labor Department's Inspector General office to log and protect confidential miner complaints, and imposes civil penalties of up to $100,000 on operators who retaliate against miners who report hazards.

Requires independent investigations of accidents involving multiple deaths or entrapments, a full-time Family Liaison to communicate with miners' families during rescues, and a rule that rescue efforts continue as long as anyone trapped could still be alive.

Requires atmospheric monitoring for carbon monoxide in underground work areas, multi-gas detectors for miners working alone, stricter seals and ventilation controls to limit explosion damage, and flame-resistant conveyor belts.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators bear the cost: buying and installing rescue chambers, communications and tracking systems, atmospheric monitors, and dust monitors; halving dust exposure in their mines; and facing much larger fines and the possibility of having their entire mine idled for repeated violations. Taxpayers fund the added federal inspectors, sampling, and studies.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is expensive: operators must install refuge chambers, leaky-feeder or wireless communication and tracking systems, atmospheric monitoring, and personal dust monitors, and the bill authorizes $30 million for the government to buy monitors alone.

The flame-resistant conveyor belt requirement exempts belts already ordered, inventoried, or installed before enactment, and belts in use more than five years that receive an annual inspection, so some older belts stay in service.

The halved dust standard and new exposure limits could be difficult for some mines to meet; the bill lets operators or miners petition the Secretary to review feasibility before a limit takes effect, an acknowledgment that compliance may strain parts of the industry.
The new Mine Safety Program Fund is financed from penalty collections rather than a direct appropriation, so enforcement spending depends on how much operators are actually fined.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: equipment, monitoring, and enforcement costs for mining companies against survival odds and long-term health for miners. The bill was written with some cost relief built in — belt exemptions, feasibility petitions, and grandfathered plans — and its strongest provisions (real rescue chambers on site, government-run dust sampling, large pattern-of-violations fines) attack the failures that killed miners in the 2006 disasters. The costs are real but targeted at an industry whose product price does not currently reflect them.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 214-199, but the Senate committee it was sent to never brought it to a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller (D-CA) introduced the S-MINER Act on June 19, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
The committee ordered the bill reported amended by a vote of 26-18 and reported it on November 15, 2007.
A Republican motion to recommit the bill with instructions to add substance abuse testing provisions failed 197-217, with 189 of 199 House Republicans in favor and 216 of 231 Democrats opposed.
The House passed the bill 214-199 on January 16, 2008: 207 of 231 Democrats voted yes and only 7 of 199 Republicans did.

The Senate received the bill on January 22, 2008 and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which took no further action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators came out ahead: they avoided the new equipment mandates, the halved dust limit, and the much larger fines. Miners gained nothing from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply by party: 207 of 231 Democrats voted yes and 16 no, while only 7 of 199 Republicans voted yes; the failed motion to recommit split the same way (8 D yea vs. 189 R yea).

industries.note: The bill would have required operators to buy and maintain rescue chambers, communication and tracking systems, atmospheric monitors, and dust monitors, cut allowable dust in half, and imposed fines up to $250,000 for patterns of violations with the power to idle an entire mine. Their compliance cost is the mirror image of miners' safety.

Mandates for refuge chambers, wireless and leaky-feeder communication and tracking systems, personal dust monitors, and atmospheric monitoring systems would create a large mandated market. The bill also directed MSHA to expedite approval of new self-rescue and communication devices.

The bill extends the conveyor belt and mine seal rules to methane-emitting metal and nonmetal mines and creates an advisory committee on extending full protections to them, so those operators face some new costs while their workers gain protections.
